summary.text: For odd \(m\) with \(\varphi(m)=2^{2^{33}}\), every prime factor must occur once and be a Fermat prime \(F_j\); the totient product then gives \(\sum_j2^j=2^{33}\), whose unique binary decomposition forces \(m=F_{33}\). The bounds \(\varphi(m)\le m\) and \(2\varphi(m)\le m\) for even \(m\) exclude all smaller candidates, while in the remaining odd case \(\varphi(F_{33})=F_{33}-1\) forces \(F_{33}\) to be prime.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\varphi\) denote Euler's totient function, and define
\[
a(n)=\min\{m\in\mathbb N:m>0\text{ and }2^n\mid \varphi(m)\}.
\]
For \(j\ge 0\), write
\[
F_j=2^{2^j}+1
\]
for the \(j\)-th Fermat number. We prove that, with
\[
N=2^{33},\qquad T=2^N=2^{2^{33}},\qquad F_{33}=T+1,
\]
one has
\[
a(N)=
\begin{cases}
F_{33},&\text{if }F_{33}\text{ is prime},\\
2^{N+1},&\text{if }F_{33}\text{ is not prime}.
\end{cases}
\]

We first establish the auxiliary facts needed for the minimality argument.

### 1. An inequality for even arguments of the totient

We claim that for every even nonnegative integer \(m\),
\[
2\varphi(m)\le m. \tag{1}
\]
For positive \(m\), this is also familiar directly from the prime-factor formula for \(\varphi\), since an even integer has the prime factor \(2\), whose factor \(1-1/2\) already reduces the totient by at least one half. Here is an elementary inductive argument that also covers all cases uniformly.

Write \(m=2r\). If \(r=0\), the assertion is immediate. Suppose \(r>0\). If \(r\) is odd, then
\[
\varphi(2r)=\varphi(r),
\]
and the general estimate \(\varphi(r)\le r\) gives
\[
2\varphi(2r)=2\varphi(r)\le 2r=m.
\]
If \(r\) is even, then
\[
\varphi(2r)=2\varphi(r).
\]
Applying the same assertion inductively to the smaller even integer \(r<2r\), we have \(2\varphi(r)\le r\), and hence
\[
2\varphi(2r)=4\varphi(r)\le 2r=m.
\]
This proves (1).

We will also use the standard facts that for every positive \(m\),
\[
0<\varphi(m)\le m, \tag{2}
\]
and if \(m>1\), then in fact
\[
\varphi(m)<m. \tag{3}
\]
Indeed, \(\varphi(m)\) counts a subset of the relevant residue classes, and when \(m>1\) not every such class is coprime to \(m\).

### 2. A structural lemma for odd integers with power-of-two totient

We prove the special statement
\[
\boxed{\text{If }m\text{ is odd and }\varphi(m)=2^{2^{33}},\text{ then }m=F_{33}.} \tag{4}
\]

Let the prime factorization of the positive odd integer \(m\) be
\[
m=\prod_{p\mid m}p^{e_p},
\]
where the product runs over the distinct prime divisors of \(m\), and every \(e_p\ge 1\). The prime-factor formula for the totient gives
\[
\varphi(m)=\prod_{p\mid m}p^{e_p-1}(p-1). \tag{5}
\]
By hypothesis, the product in (5) is a power of \(2\). Every individual factor in that product therefore divides a power of \(2\).

Fix a prime divisor \(p\) of \(m\). Since \(m\) is odd, \(p\ne 2\). We first show that \(e_p=1\). If \(e_p\ge 2\), then \(p\) divides \(p^{e_p-1}(p-1)\), and consequently \(p\) divides \(\varphi(m)=2^{2^{33}}\). A prime dividing a power of \(2\) must be \(2\), contradicting \(p\ne2\). Thus
\[
e_p=1. \tag{6}
\]

It follows as well from (5) that \(p-1\) divides a power of \(2\), so
\[
p-1=2^r
\]
for some \(r\ge0\). Since \(p\) is odd, \(p\ne2\), and hence \(r>0\). Thus
\[
p=2^r+1. \tag{7}
\]
Because \(p\) is prime, the exponent \(r\) must itself be a power of \(2\). To see this, factor \(r\) as
\[
r=2^j u
\]
with \(u\) odd. If \(u>1\), put \(x=2^{2^j}\). Then
\[
2^r+1=x^u+1.
\]
For odd \(u>1\), the integer \(x^u+1\) has the proper factor \(x+1\), because
\[
x^u+1=(x+1)(x^{u-1}-x^{u-2}+\cdots-x+1).
\]
That would make \(2^r+1=p\) composite. Therefore \(u=1\), so \(r=2^j\) and
\[
p=2^{2^j}+1=F_j. \tag{8}
\]
Consequently, every prime divisor of \(m\) occurs to the first power and is a Fermat number \(F_j\) which is prime.

Let \(J\) be the finite set of indices \(j\) arising from the distinct prime divisors of \(m\). Distinct prime divisors give distinct indices: if \(F_i=F_j\), then
\(2^{2^i}=2^{2^j}\), whence \(2^i=2^j\) and therefore \(i=j\). By (5), (6), and (8),
\[
\varphi(m)=\prod_{j\in J}(F_j-1)
=\prod_{j\in J}2^{2^j}
=2^{\sum_{j\in J}2^j}.
\]
On the other hand, \(\varphi(m)=2^{2^{33}}\). Since powers of \(2\) have unique exponents,
\[
\sum_{j\in J}2^j=2^{33}. \tag{9}
\]

We now show that (9) forces
\[
J=\{33\}. \tag{10}
\]
First, every \(j\in J\) satisfies \(j\le33\), since its positive summand \(2^j\) is at most the whole sum \(2^{33}\). If \(33\notin J\), then \(J\subseteq\{0,1,\ldots,32\}\), and therefore
\[
\sum_{j\in J}2^j\le\sum_{j=0}^{32}2^j=2^{33}-1,
\]
contrary to (9). Thus \(33\in J\). But the term indexed by \(33\) already contributes the entire amount \(2^{33}\) in (9), and every other summand is positive. Hence no other index can belong to \(J\), proving (10).

Thus \(m\) has exactly one prime divisor, namely \(F_{33}\), and that divisor occurs with exponent one. Therefore
\[
m=F_{33},
\]
which proves the structural assertion (4).

### 3. A useful reduction below \(2^{N+1}\)

Suppose \(m>0\), \(T=2^N\) divides \(\varphi(m)\), and
\[
m<2^{N+1}=2T.
\]
Write
\[
\varphi(m)=Tk
\]
for some integer \(k\ge0\). Positivity of \(\varphi(m)\) implies \(k\ge1\). By (2),
\[
Tk=\varphi(m)\le m<2T.
\]
Since \(T>0\), this gives \(k<2\). Thus \(k=1\), and so
\[
\varphi(m)=T=2^N. \tag{11}
\]
In words: any admissible integer strictly below \(2^{N+1}\) must have totient exactly \(2^N\), not a larger multiple of it.

We also note that \(2^{N+1}\) itself is always admissible. The prime-power formula for the totient gives
\[
\varphi(2^{N+1})=2^{N+1}-2^N=2^N=T. \tag{12}
\]
Thus \(T\mid\varphi(2^{N+1})\), and in particular
\[
a(N)\le 2^{N+1}. \tag{13}
\]

### 4. The case in which \(F_{33}\) is prime

Assume first that
\[
F_{33}=T+1
\]
is prime. Then
\[
\varphi(F_{33})=F_{33}-1=T.
\]
Therefore \(F_{33}\) is admissible, and
\[
a(N)\le F_{33}. \tag{14}
\]

It remains to show that no smaller positive integer is admissible. Suppose, to the contrary, that \(m<F_{33}=T+1\), that \(m>0\), and that \(T\mid\varphi(m)\). Since \(m\) and \(T\) are integers,
\[
m<T+1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad m\le T. \tag{15}
\]
Write \(\varphi(m)=Tk\). Positivity of \(\varphi(m)\) gives \(k\ge1\), so
\[
\varphi(m)\ge T. \tag{16}
\]
Combining (2), (15), and (16), we obtain
\[
T\le\varphi(m)\le m\le T.
\]
In particular, \(m\ge T\). Since \(T=2^{2^{33}}>2\), we have \(m>1\), and hence the strict inequality (3) says \(\varphi(m)<m\). This contradicts the displayed chain, which forces \(\varphi(m)=m=T\).

Thus no admissible positive integer is smaller than \(F_{33}\). Together with (14), this yields
\[
a(N)=F_{33}
\]
when \(F_{33}\) is prime.

### 5. The case in which \(F_{33}\) is not prime

Now assume that \(F_{33}\) is not prime. By (12), \(2^{N+1}\) is admissible, so (13) gives
\[
a(N)\le2^{N+1}.
\]
We prove the reverse inequality by showing that no positive admissible \(m\) can be strictly smaller than \(2^{N+1}\).

Suppose, for contradiction, that
\[
m>0,\qquad T\mid\varphi(m),\qquad m<2^{N+1}=2T. \tag{17}
\]
By the reduction (11),
\[
\varphi(m)=T=2^{2^{33}}. \tag{18}
\]
We divide into the two parity cases.

#### Even case

If \(m\) is even, inequality (1) and (18) give
\[
2T=2\varphi(m)\le m.
\]
But \(2T=2^{N+1}\), contradicting the strict inequality \(m<2^{N+1}\) in (17). Hence an admissible counterexample below \(2^{N+1}\) cannot be even.

#### Odd case

If \(m\) is odd, (18) and the structural lemma (4) imply
\[
m=F_{33}. \tag{19}
\]
Substituting this into (18), and using \(F_{33}-1=T\), gives
\[
\varphi(F_{33})=T=F_{33}-1. \tag{20}
\]
For an integer \(q>1\), the equality \(\varphi(q)=q-1\) holds exactly when \(q\) is prime. Indeed, if \(q\) is prime, every integer from \(1\) through \(q-1\) is coprime to \(q\), so \(\varphi(q)=q-1\). Conversely, if \(q\) is composite, it has a proper divisor \(d\) with \(1<d<q\); then \(d\) is not coprime to \(q\), so not all of \(1,\ldots,q-1\) are counted by the totient and \(\varphi(q)<q-1\).

Since \(F_{33}>2\), equation (20) therefore implies that \(F_{33}\) is prime. This contradicts the assumption of the present case. Thus an admissible counterexample below \(2^{N+1}\) cannot be odd either.

Both parity cases being impossible, every positive \(m\) satisfying \(T\mid\varphi(m)\) obeys
\[
m\ge2^{N+1}.
\]
Together with the admissibility of \(2^{N+1}\), this proves
\[
a(N)=2^{N+1}
\]
when \(F_{33}\) is not prime.

Finally, restoring \(N=2^{33}\), we conclude
\[
\boxed{
a(2^{33})=
\begin{cases}
F_{33}=2^{2^{33}}+1,&\text{if }F_{33}\text{ is prime},\\[2mm]
2^{2^{33}+1},&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}}
\]
